The Add. Table well turns measures into extra cells drawn beside the marks — a summary column, a mean, a base size, a logo, anything that belongs next to the chart rather than inside it. It works in every layout, and follows it: in the Bar, Stacked Bar and 100% Stacked Bar modes the fields are drawn as columns beside the bars, lined up with the bands of the category axis, so each value sits on its own row; in the Column, Stacked Column and 100% Stacked Column modes they become rows of cells, each one centered under its category. The field names run down the left of the chart instead of across the top. Each field also chooses which side of the chart it is drawn on — see Before or after the chart.

Drop one measure per column into Add. Table. The order of the well is the order of the columns, left to right; the measure name becomes the column header. Values are formatted with the measure's own Power BI format string, so a percentage stays a percentage and a currency keeps its symbol — nothing to configure.

Formatting is per column, so it does not fit the standard formatting pane. In edit mode a gear icon appears in the top-right corner of the visual and opens the column editor, one block per column, in the official Power BI dialog: Section What it holds Format Font family, size and color, bold / italic / underline, whether the header is shown, the Position of the column — before or after the chart — and its size: Column Width in the bar layouts, Row Height in the column layouts (0 = fitted to the font or the logo). Only the dimension that applies to the current layout is offered Row box / Column box A frame that makes the whole row (or column) stand out — see Row and column box Logo Whether the column holds a picture rather than a value, and how big to draw it — see Logo columns Separator A rule drawn on the leading edge of the column — a vertical one on its left in the bar layouts, a horizontal one above the row in the column layouts — and its color Warning threshold Low and high thresholds decorating the value — see Thresholds Critical threshold Blanks the row, keeps only the value, or marks it — see Thresholds Sections are collapsible; Format opens by default. At the bottom of the dialog, a JSON box shows the whole configuration: it can be copied to another report, or pasted back in to apply a set of columns in one go. Where it is stored The editor writes its JSON into the Add. Table → Column Format (JSON) property of the formatting pane. Editing it by hand there works too, but the gear icon is the comfortable way. Renaming a measure keeps its formatting: when exactly one column disappears and exactly one appears, the visual treats it as a rename and moves the settings over.

Position, in the Format section, decides which side of the chart a field is drawn on. It is set per field, so a logo can sit in front of the bar while the base size stays behind it. Position Bar layouts Column layouts After the chart (default) to the right of the bars below the columns, above the category labels Before the chart between the category labels and the bars above the columns The category labels always stay on the outside: in Before mode they move over to make room, they are never covered. Space is reserved on both sides, so widening a column narrows the plot area rather than pushing anything out of the visual.

The box section frames a whole row (column layouts) or a whole column (bar layouts), its header included, to make it easier to read across — a base row in a light grey band, a key indicator outlined in the brand colour. A field can carry a picture instead of a value — a brand logo next to each category, a flag, a small pictogram. The image is a base64 string, exactly like the one the threshold markers accept. In the Logo section, Content chooses how the field is read: Auto (default) — the field is painted as an image when Power BI already knows it is one: its Data category is set to Image URL in the model, or its values start with data:image/. Otherwise it is text. In most cases there is nothing to change here. Always an image (base64) — for a field holding a bare base64 blob, with no data:image/png;base64, prefix and no data category. Such a value is indistinguishable from ordinary text, so Auto cannot recognise it. Always text — forces the value to be written out, whatever the model says.

You give one dimension and the picture keeps its proportions: Height (width adapts) (default) — Size is the height in pixels; the width follows the image's aspect ratio. Width (height adapts) — Size is the width; the height follows. The free dimension is still bounded by the cell — the column width and the band thickness in the bar layouts, the band width and the row height in the column layouts. A picture so far out of proportion that it would spill onto the bars or onto its neighbour is scaled down to fit instead. tip Logos read best before the chart: the picture then sits right between the category label and its bar.

Each column carries two independent threshold levels, both off by default. They exist for one recurring need in survey reporting: a result computed on too small a base should be flagged — or not published at all. Cell value What happens between the critical and the low warning threshold, or over the high one the value is decorated — marker, colour, pill below the critical threshold the critical treatment applies — by default the whole row is blanked Thresholds are compared strictly: a value equal to a threshold is not flagged. Only numeric cells are tested; a blank or textual value never triggers anything.

Tick Low threshold (value under) and / or High threshold (value over) and set their values. A cell outside the range is then decorated with any mix of: a Marker next to the value — Text (an emoticon, an exclamation mark, a short sentence… with its own color), Image (base64) (pasted with or without the data:image/png;base64, prefix), or No marker. Marker size is the font size of a text, the height of an image; Color the value — the value itself is written in the chosen color; Pill behind the value — a rounded background behind the value, with its color and transparency. The marker is drawn to the right of the value, and the pair stays centered in the cell.

Tick Critical threshold, set the value, then pick what happens under it: Blank the whole row (default) — the row is removed from the chart entirely: no bars, no data labels, no logos, no error bars, no tooltip, and no value in any additional column, not just this one. What remains is the category label, drawn as usual on the axis, and a replacement message centered on the row — typically "Base faible". The message may be left empty, in which case the row simply stays blank. The value axis is rescaled on the rows that survive, so a hidden row no longer stretches the scale of the whole chart. Blank the row except this value — the row is blanked the same way, but this value stays, written in the critical color next to the replacement message. Saying a base is too small is good; showing how far it is from the threshold is sometimes better. Text next to the value / Image next to the value — the row is kept as it is and the value is marked, like the warning level but with its own text, image, size and color. One column can blank a row for all the others A row is blanked as soon as one column asks for it. Put the critical threshold on the column that carries the base, and every other column on that row goes away with it.

Repeating the same sentence on each band would be noise. When all the rows are blanked, the visual draws the message once, centered on the whole chart. The additional table is not drawn at all — no headers, no reserved space on either side — and the value axis disappears with the bars. The category axis stays: those categories are still perfectly valid, they simply have nothing publishable to show.

documents.t: A satisfaction chart with three additional columns — a top-2-boxes percentage, a mean, and the base — where results computed on fewer than 1 700 respondents must not be published: Put the three measures in Add. Table. Open the gear icon, expand Critical threshold on the Base column. Tick Critical threshold, set Critical when value is under to 1700, leave Then on Blank the whole row, and type Base faible as the replacement message. Still on Base, expand Warning threshold, tick Low threshold, set it to 2000 and pick a small warning image or a ⚠ text marker — or tick Pill behind the value to highlight the base itself. Rows under 1 700 now show only their label and Base faible; rows between 1 700 and 2 000 keep their bars and carry the warning marker next to the base.

The space reserved beside the chart is the sum of the column widths (or of the row heights in the column layouts), so widening a column narrows the plot area rather than pushing anything out of the visual. In the bar layouts, headers wrap over at most three lines and are truncated with an ellipsis beyond that; the space above the plot area grows to fit the tallest header. In the column layouts they are single-line, right-aligned in the left margin, and truncated past a third of the chart width. A measure that returns no value for a given category leaves the cell empty — it does not count as a threshold breach.

You can drag two or more fields into the Axis data well to create a hierarchical category axis. The visual renders each bar group at the leaf level (innermost field) and draws bracket labels below the axis for every parent level. Example: drag Country then Planet into Axis: Individual bars are labeled by Planet (the leaf field) A bracketed span below groups them by Country (the parent field) Vertical separators mark the boundaries between countries

When multiple fields are in the Axis well, Power BI's drill-down controls activate in the visual header: Control Behaviour Drill down (chevron ▼) Shows only the next level — one field at a time Drill up (chevron ▲) Returns to the previous level Expand all (two chevrons ▼▼) Shows all levels simultaneously with bracketed group labels Just need "None" and "Other" at the end? A hierarchy is not required for that. Use First items / Last items in the Bar Settings card to pin those categories to either end of the axis, in the order you choose. Field order matters Place the outermost group (e.g. Country) first in the Axis well and the leaf items (e.g. Planet) last. The visual always uses the last field as the individual bar labels and all preceding fields as parent group brackets.

Categories such as None, Other or Not specified rarely belong in the middle of a chart sorted by value. First items and Last items pin the categories you name to the start or the end of the axis, and keep every other bar in its natural order. Type the labels separated by commas: Aucun, Autre Both fields accept several labels, and the order you type them is the order they are displayed in: Setting Value Result Last items Autre, Aucun …other bars…, Autre, Aucun Last items Aucun, Autre …other bars…, Aucun, Autre First items Ensemble Ensemble, …other bars…

Order is preserved — items are placed in the order you list them, not alphabetically. Everything else is untouched — unlisted categories keep the sort applied to the visual (by measure descending, alphabetical, or the model's own sort order). First wins — a label typed in both fields is pinned to the start. Matching ignores case and surrounding spaces, but the label must otherwise match the axis label exactly. Unknown labels are ignored — a typo or a category filtered out of the current page simply has no effect.

The comma is the separator, so a label that contains one must be wrapped in double quotes: "Aucun, ne se prononce pas", Autre To include a double quote inside a quoted label, type it twice: "Il dit ""oui""".

Chart type First items Last items Column and Stacked Column (vertical) Left Right Bar and Stacked Bar (horizontal) Top Bottom Pinning a whole group With a multi-level axis, typing a parent group value pins every bar of that group. Pinning is applied before the grouping, so pinned bars leave their original position and move as a block. Conditional formatting Both fields support the fx button, so the list of labels can come from a measure returning text instead of being typed by hand — useful when the categories to push to the end depend on the report context.

A scrollbar inside a report tile hides entries behind a control nobody thinks to drag, so it was removed outright. Entries that no longer fit With scrolling gone, a legend taller than the space it has is clipped rather than scrolled. Wrap makes entries taller and so clips sooner than Ellipsis — give the legend a horizontal position, or shorten the labels, when every series has to stay visible.

The Significance card runs up to three independent statistical tests over the chart and decorates the bars whose difference from a reference is statistically significant. It is the same card as the Line Chart — same modes, same statistics, shared with the SDM Smart Table — with display modes suited to bars.

Optional. Significance reference Measure One to three measures read by the External reference mode. Not drawn. Optional. The Significance card appears in the Format pane as soon as a Base or a Significance reference measure is bound.

Axis — One or more categorical fields for bar grouping. Adding multiple fields creates a multi-level hierarchy axis with drill-down support. When two or more fields are placed in the Axis well, the visual activates Power BI's drill-down icon in the visual header and renders a hierarchical axis: Drill down / Drill up — Navigate one level at a time Expand all — Show all levels simultaneously, with bracketed group labels and optional separator lines below the axis See Multi-Level Axis for full details and formatting options.

Clicking on bars cross-filters other visuals on the report page. Action Behavior Click a bar Selects that single data point Ctrl+Click (Cmd+Click on Mac) Adds or removes individual bars from the selection Alt+Click a bar Selects all bars of the same series (Legend value) across every category Click empty area Clears the selection Alt+Click is only available when a Legend field is assigned. It is useful for cross-filtering an entire series at once rather than selecting bars one by one.

The Animation card plays an entrance animation when the chart appears: the data is drawn, then the labels fade in. Setting Description Animation (card toggle) Turns the animation on or off. On by default. Type Fade: the whole visual fades in at once. Grow (default): the axes and the legend fade in, the data is drawn (see the table below), then the data labels, significance markers, base row, Add. Table and Note fade in. Cascade: a variant of Grow, see below. Duration (ms) Duration of the whole animation, from 100 to 5000 ms. 800 ms by default. The labels start fading in halfway through the drawing and end with it.

The animation plays only when the data changes: when the report opens, when a filter or a slicer is changed, or when a drill-down level changes. It does not replay when you: resize the visual; change a setting in the Format pane; select a series or a point. It is never played: during an export to PDF or PowerPoint (Power BI service and Desktop), or when a subscription e-mail is rendered. The visual is drawn in its final state straight away, so exports are not slowed down; when the viewer's operating system asks for reduced motion (an accessibility setting in Windows, macOS, iOS and Android).

Chart Grow Cascade Line Chart the lines are drawn from left to right the lines are drawn one after the other Column Chart the columns grow from the zero line (negative ones downwards); bars grow from left to right same as Grow Scatter the points expand from the centre of the plot the points are uncovered from left to right Pie / Donut the slices open like a fan, over the chart's real angle (half circles included) the pies of a small multiple open one after the other Radar the series expand from the centre same as Grow Gradient Heatmap the surface and its isolines are uncovered from left to right uncovered from top to bottom

The Global Threshold card covers the two situations where a visual should not be drawn at all: no data left after the filters, and a result that must not be published — a base too small, a period still being collected, an unusable slicer selection. In both cases the visual erases itself and, optionally, paints a message in its place. Available everywhere All six visuals — Column, Line, Scatter, Gradient Heatmap, Radar and Pie — expose the card under the name Global Threshold, with the conditional test described below.

Property Description Default Empty Panel Whether the message is painted when the dataset comes back empty. On Message Text drawn when the dataset is empty. Leave it empty for a completely blank panel. Supports conditional formatting (fx). No Data to display Conditional Message Text drawn when the test below is met. Leave it empty for a completely blank panel. Supports conditional formatting (fx). Not enough data to display Test if Left operand of the test — usually a measure bound through fx: a base, a count of respondents. 0 Is Comparison operator: <, = or >. < To Right operand of the test. 0 Horizontal Alignment Left, center or right. Center Vertical Alignment Top, middle or bottom. Middle Font Font family, size, and bold / italic / underline. The size supports conditional formatting (fx). Segoe UI, 14 pt Text Color Message color. Supports conditional formatting (fx). #333333 Background Color Fill painted behind the message. Supports conditional formatting (fx). #FFFFFF Transparency Background transparency, 0 % (opaque) to 100 % (invisible). Supports conditional formatting (fx). 100 % Why the background looks like nothing at first Transparency defaults to 100 %, so the panel is transparent out of the box and the report page shows through. Lower it to make Background Color visible.

When the filters of the page leave no row at all, the visual always erases itself — bars, lines, points, axes, legend, data labels, analytics overlays and tooltips. Drawing a pair of empty axes reads as a broken component, so this is not optional. Empty Panel only decides whether Message is painted over the blank visual: On (default) — the message explains the situation: "Data not available for this period". Off — the visual is simply blank, no text at all. An empty Message gives the same result as switching the toggle off: a truly blank panel — useful to reserve space in a layout, or to hide a chart without leaving a hole marked by an error. The visual keeps its position and size on the page: the layout does not reflow, the frame stays where it is. Data fields stay bound, so the chart comes straight back as soon as the filters return rows — nothing is lost.

The second block replaces the visual when a test holds, on a dataset that does have rows. Its typical use is a confidentiality threshold: a base too small to be published. The test is Test if Is To — for example Test if [Base] Is < To 30. It fires on its own: it does not depend on the Empty Panel toggle. When it holds, the chart is erased exactly as above and Conditional Message is painted instead. Both operands carry the fx button, so the left one is normally bound to a measure: Base = COUNTROWS ( Respondents ) Bind [Base] to Test if, leave Is on <, set To to 30, and the visual hides itself whenever the current filter context leaves fewer than 30 respondents. Constant operands Both operands default to 0 with the < operator, a test that is never true — which is why the conditional message stays off until you actually configure it.

The two cases are exclusive and evaluated in this order: Dataset empty → the chart is erased; Message is painted if Empty Panel is on. Dataset not empty, test met → the chart is erased; Conditional Message is painted. Otherwise → the chart is drawn normally. The conditional test is only evaluated when there is data: an empty dataset never shows the conditional message.

This card hides the entire visual. To hide only the rows whose base is too small — keeping the others, and their category labels, visible — use the per-column thresholds of the Add. Table instead. The two work well together: a per-column critical threshold for the individual rows, this card for the case where the whole visual has nothing publishable left. The Pie Chart, which has no additional columns to threshold, answers the same need one chart at a time with its Series Threshold card: the smallest base of a small multiple decides whether that chart is flagged, or withdrawn and replaced by a message, while the rest of the grid keeps being drawn.
documents.s: A whole-visual threshold, not a per-row one

documents.t: The panel never intercepts clicks: it lets pointer events through, so the report page keeps behaving normally underneath. The visual signals to Power BI that rendering is finished as soon as the panel is drawn, so the page stops loading and Export to PDF or Print does not wait on a visual that will never draw. The About icon, the settings gear where a visual has one, and the Powered by Socio Data Management watermark of the Free edition all remain visible above the panel. See Licensing. The message accepts line breaks and wraps on the width of the visual; text that exceeds the available height is clipped rather than overflowing.

The significance tests of the charts compare what the chart shows: a point with the previous category, with a reference category or with a reference series. Very often, though, the reference is something the chart does not show — last year, a benchmark, the total of another scope. Loading that data into the visual only to hide it would go against the way the SDM charts work: they receive figures already computed by the model and draw them. The External reference test mode answers that need. You drop in the Significance reference data role a measure that returns, for each point of the chart, the reference that point must be compared with. The visual reads it and decorates the point with the display settings of the test. Available in the Column Chart, the Line Chart, the Radar and the Pie Chart.

Power BI evaluates the reference measure in the same filter context as the point it goes with: same category, same legend value. A measure computing last year's score therefore returns, for every point, that point's last-year score — each brand against its own N-1, each quarter against its own quarter one year earlier. There is nothing to pair by hand, and the N-1 rows do not have to be in the visual: the report can be filtered on the current year.
documents.s: How the reference is paired with the point

documents.t: A short JSON text. Four formats are accepted, from "compute everything" to "just display my result": JSON What the visual does Needs on the displayed point {"val": 0.42, "n": 2574} Proportion test between the point and val, with bases n₁ (the point's Base) and n Base {"val": 3.87, "n": 2574, "stddev": 0.33} Mean test between the point and val Base and Standard Deviation {"ttest": 2.31} Compares the statistic you computed with the level of the card: 1.645 / 1.96 / 2.58 at 90 / 95 / 99 % nothing {"signif": -1} Displays your result as is: -1 lower, 0 not significant, 1 higher nothing Sign convention For ttest and signif, a positive value means the displayed point is higher than the reference: compute ttest = (displayed − reference) / se, not the other way round. With the opposite convention every decoration comes out reversed — without any error message. {"signif"} is not limited to statistics: any rule computed in the model (a business threshold, an in-house test) can use the icons, texts and colours of the chart.

The format is read on the first readable value of each series and applies to the whole series. A value in another format in the same series is counted as invalid and left undecorated. A blank measure means "no test on this point" — it is not an error. Likewise, a point whose displayed value is blank is never tested, whatever the format — even a given ttest or signif.

The visual accepts what DAX string building usually produces: keys in any case, with aliases: val / value, n / base, stddev / sd, ttest / t, signif / s; single quotes, unquoted keys, ; as a separator; numbers written as strings, with a decimal point or a decimal comma: {"val": "0,42"}. The only thing that cannot be read is a decimal comma outside quotes — {"val": 0,42} cannot be told apart from a separator. Build numbers with FORMAT(x, "0.##########", "en-US"), which always writes a decimal point whatever the locale of the report, or put them in quotes.

Proportion vs. last year — the visual runs the test: Signif ref N-1 = VAR v = CALCULATE ( [Satisfaction %], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) ) VAR n = CALCULATE ( [Base], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) ) RETURN IF ( NOT ISBLANK ( v ) && n > 0, "{""val"":" & FORMAT ( v, "0.##########", "en-US" ) & ",""n"":" & FORMAT ( n, "0", "en-US" ) & "}" ) Mean vs. a benchmark scope — add the standard deviation: Signif ref benchmark = VAR scope = REMOVEFILTERS ( Brand ) VAR m = CALCULATE ( [Average score], scope ) VAR n = CALCULATE ( [Base], scope ) VAR sd = CALCULATE ( [Std dev score], scope ) RETURN "{""val"":" & FORMAT ( m, "0.##########", "en-US" ) & ",""n"":" & FORMAT ( n, "0", "en-US" ) & ",""stddev"":" & FORMAT ( sd, "0.##########", "en-US" ) & "}" Statistic or result computed in the model: Signif ref t = "{""ttest"":" & FORMAT ( [My t statistic], "0.####", "en-US" ) & "}" Signif ref rule = "{""signif"":" & SWITCH ( TRUE (), [Delta] > 0.05, 1, [Delta] < -0.05, -1, 0 ) & "}" One measure, several visuals The string building is the tedious part. If your Power BI version supports DAX user-defined functions, write it once — for example SignifRef ( value, base, stddev ) — and call it from each reference measure.

Drop the reference measure(s) in Significance reference — up to three, one per test if needed. In the Significance card, set Test N to External reference. In the Test N group: Property Description Default Reference measure (regex) Which measure of the Significance reference well this test uses, by its name (empty — the first one) Apply to measure (regex) Which displayed measure(s) the test decorates, by name (empty — every measure) Apply to measure matters when several measures are in Values: the reference measure is evaluated per category and per legend value, but it cannot know which displayed measure it is being compared with. Give each test its own target — test 1 on Gross Margin with an N-1 reference, test 2 on Net Margin with another one. Both fields are case-insensitive regular expressions matched anywhere in the name (N-1, ^Score$, Gross|Net).

The status line of the test reports what was read, with symbols and JSON keys only: Status Meaning ✓ "Score N-1" {val, n} · 24 points Measure found, format detected, 24 points compared … · 3 not testable Readable values that could not be tested — base, value or standard deviation missing on the displayed point … · ⚠ 2 invalid Values that could not be read, or in another format than the series' one ✗ no measure in the reference well The Significance reference role is empty ✗ no reference measure matches Reference measure matches no measure of the well ✗ "…" — no displayed measure matches Apply to measure matches no displayed measure ✗ "…" — no readable value The measure returned nothing that parses ⚠ invalid regex One of the two patterns does not compile In the Line Chart, the Show calculation (debug) toggle also lists every external comparison, with its operands or its given statistic.
The pie tests shares (slice / series total). With {"val", "n"}, val must therefore be a share on 0..1 as well. {"val", "n", "stddev"} is compared with the raw slice value, as the Means test does.

The Note card draws a caption box over the chart — a base, a source, a reading key, a warning. Its text is not just static: it can compute values from the fields already placed in the visual, and it can switch to an alert wording when a threshold is crossed. Available everywhere All six visuals expose the card — Column Chart, Line Chart, Scatter Plot, Gradient Heatmap, Radar and Pie Chart — with the same properties and the same behavior everywhere. It replaces the Line Chart’s former Cartouche card, which did the same job in a simpler way and has been removed: the Note adds formulas over the fields, an alert state, and a band of its own so the lines and the legend are pushed out of its way instead of being drawn under it. A report that used the Cartouche keeps opening, but its caption is no longer drawn — set it up again here.

The Text property accepts free text mixed with formulas over any field placed in the visual — the field name is the one shown in the field well: Formula Result %MIN(field) Smallest value of the field %MAX(field) Largest value of the field %COUNT(field) Number of values %AVG(field) Mean of the values %SUM(field) Sum of the values Base : %MIN(base_rep) to %MAX(base_rep) respondents A field name that matches nothing renders as #NAME?, and a formula with no usable value renders as #N/A — both are visible on the chart rather than silent, so a typo is caught immediately. Display Units and Decimals control how those computed numbers are written. Thousands are grouped when nothing is abbreviated, so a base reads as 2 577.

Text can also be bound to a measure with the fx button. A numeric measure then arrives as a raw number, and is written with the Display Units and Decimals of the card — floating-point noise included, so a base resolving to 2576.9999999 still reads 2 577. The wording comes from Prefix and Suffix instead: Property Description Prefix Placed in front of the text Suffix Placed after the text — a unit, a closing parenthesis This is what removes the string measure that used to be written once per visual: Before two measures per visual: BaseCount (numeric, for the test) "Base: " & BaseCount (text, for the display) After one measure: BaseCount → Text (fx) one setting: "Base: " → Prefix Translating a report Prefix and Suffix are ordinary visual settings, so a report translator that handles visual settings picks them up. Translating "Base: " in 50 visuals beats rewriting 50 DAX measures. Both are bindable through fx as well, if the wording has to come from the model. Prefix and Suffix word the normal value, and the alert keeps them: by default an Alert text is added after the caption. Only the Replace the text mode drops them along with the value they were wording — “Base: Base too small” would make no sense. The alert Prefix pictogram stays leftmost either way.
documents.s: Prefix and Suffix — one measure instead of two

documents.t: Property Description Default Position Top or Bottom, each in Left / Center / Right Top (Right) Horizontal margin Distance from the left or right edge 8 Vertical margin Distance from the top or bottom edge 4 Padding Space between the border and the text 2 The Note is not painted over the chart: the band it occupies is reserved, and the plot — along with the legend — is pushed out of its way. When a horizontal legend sits in the same band, the two share the line if they are in different zones; otherwise the whole Note box is reserved on top of the legend, and the legend stays the closer of the two to the chart.

A Note is neutral until you ask for a box: it is drawn as plain text over the chart, with neither fill nor outline. Two toggles decide otherwise, and the colors below each one are only read once its toggle is on. Property Description Default Font Family, size, bold, italic, underline Segoe UI 10, italic Text Color Color of the caption #333333 Background Whether the box is filled Off Background Color / Transparency Fill of the box — 0 % is opaque, 100 % invisible White, 0 % Border Whether the box is outlined Off Border Color / Width / Corner Radius Outline of the box #CCCCCC, 1, 2

The alert swaps the appearance of the Note as soon as a condition is met — typically a base falling under a publication threshold. Property Description Alert Master toggle of the alert block Test if Left operand: a number, or a formula such as %MIN(base_rep) Test if (measure) The same operand, when it has to come from a measure. Used when Test if is left empty Is Comparison operator: <, = or > To Right operand Alert text Shown while the alert holds. Leave empty to keep the normal text alone. Formulas are accepted here too. Alert Text Mode Add after the text (default) keeps the value, its prefix and its suffix, and adds the alert sentence after them. Replace the text swaps the whole caption for it. Prefix Placed before everything while the alert holds — usually a pictogram such as ⚠️ Background / Border Whether the alert draws a filled and outlined box, on by default Text / Background / Border Color Colors used while the alert holds In Add after the text mode, a single space is inserted between the caption and the alert sentence unless one of the two already brings its own separator, so typing — base too small reads correctly without double spacing: Base: 175 respondents — base too small Because Test if accepts a formula, the alert reacts to the data actually plotted rather than to a fixed value: Test if %MIN(base_rep) Is < To 50 Alert text ⚠️ Base too small — results are indicative only Why there are two Test if boxes A Power BI setting is declared with a single data type, and the fx field picker only offers fields of that type. Test if is a text box — that is what lets it hold 10 or %MIN(base_rep) — so its picker lists text fields only, and a measure returning a number cannot be chosen there. Test if (measure) is the numeric counterpart, and the one to bind a measure to. It is read whenever Test if is left empty, so fill in one or the other. The same measure can then feed the displayed value and the threshold: bind it to Text and to Test if (measure), with the wording in Prefix. If the measure is already in one of the visual's field wells, you can skip the second box altogether and name it in a formula — %MIN(My measure) — in Test if. The alert draws its own box A Note is plain text by default, so the alert carries its own Background and Border toggles rather than inheriting the ones in Style — otherwise its colors would never be reachable. Both are on, which means enabling the alert and crossing the threshold gives you the colored box straight away. Turn them off for a text-only alert, signalled by the text color and the pictogram alone.

The two cards answer different questions and can be used together: Global Threshold Note What it does Erases the chart and paints a message in its place Adds a caption next to a chart that is still drawn When to use it The result must not be published at all The result is publishable but needs a caveat A common pairing is an alert Note under a moderate base, and the Global Threshold under a base too small to show anything. On the Pie Chart a third card sits between the two: the Series Threshold asks the same question of each small multiple on its own, so one market can be withdrawn without taking the others with it.

The Series Color data role allows you to control series colors directly from your data model. Simply create a column or measure that returns a hex color code: SeriesColor = SWITCH( SELECTEDVALUE(Products[Category]), "Electronics", "#4682B4", "Clothing", "#FF6347", "Food", "#32CD32", "#888888" ) The role is called Color on the scatter plot. The Gradient Heatmap has none — its colors come from the color scale instead. On the radar and the pie chart the role feeds one dimension at a time, chosen by the Apply colors to dropdown of the visual's main card.
Colors are resolved in this order: Per-series conditional formatting (fx) from Power BI seriesColor data role value Host color palette Default 10-color array

The Logo data role accepts base64-encoded images. If the value doesn't start with data:, the visual automatically prepends data:image/png;base64,. Logos can appear in: The legend (column, line, scatter, radar and pie) End-of-line labels (line chart) Inside bars (column chart) At the outer end of each axis (radar) In the title of each small multiple (pie chart) The Gradient Heatmap has no Logo role.

Open your Power BI report In the Visualizations pane, click the ... Five of the six SDM Smart Graph Visuals support data-driven series colors and series logos — every one except the Gradient Heatmap, whose colors come from its color scale. Instead of relying on Power BI's default color palette and plain text legends, you can control the exact color and display a custom logo for each series — directly from your data model. This is one of the key differentiators of the SDM Smart Graph Visuals compared to Power BI's built-in charts.

Feature Column Line Scatter Radar Pie Series Color Yes Yes Yes (role named Color) Yes Yes Logo in legend Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Logo in bars Yes — — — — Logo in end-of-line labels — Yes — — — Logo at the end of each axis — — — Yes — Logo in the small-multiple title — — — — Yes Colors applied to a choice of dimension — — — Yes Yes
The recommended approach is to create a lookup table containing one row per series, with a color column and a logo column.

Create a table (in Excel or any data source) with at least three columns: Column Description Example label The series identifier (must match your Legend field values) Earth color Hex RGB color code #4682B4 logo Base64-encoded image data:image/png;base64,iVBOR... Color Format Colors must be expressed in hexadecimal RGB format (e.g. #FF6347). Other formats like rgb(255,99,71) or color names like red are not supported. Base64 Image Encoding Logo images must be Base64-encoded. You can generate Base64 strings using: AI tools — Ask an AI assistant to generate a simple icon as base64 Free online converters — Search for "image to base64 converter" GIMP plugins — Export as base64 from GIMP The Python script provided below in this guide
Import the lookup table into your Power BI model alongside your main data table.

documents.t: Create two measures in your destination table to look up the color and logo for each series: planet_color = LOOKUPVALUE( LogosColors[color], LogosColors[Planet.label], SELECTEDVALUE(Customer_Satisfaction[Planet.Label]) ) planet_logo = LOOKUPVALUE( LogosColors[logo], LogosColors[Planet.label], SELECTEDVALUE(Customer_Satisfaction[Planet.Label]) )
Drag your color measure into the Series Color data well and your logo measure into the Logo data well.

When configured correctly, Power BI displays the resolved data as a matrix: Rows — correspond to the Axis field (e.g. Country.label) Column headers — correspond to the Legend field (e.g. Planet.Label) For each combination, the visual receives the value from the Values field, the color from the Series Color measure, and the logo from the Logo measure.

This is the single most common source of surprise, because Power BI binds the two very differently — and it does so silently. You drop a… Power BI binds it as It attaches to Use it for Column A grouping, joined to the category axis The category A color or a logo that is an attribute of the category itself Measure A value, evaluated inside each legend group The legend value A color or a logo that identifies the series A column only works when it lines up row for row with the category axis. Drop a column that describes another dimension — a country flag while the categories are brands — and Power BI cross-joins the two: the category axis becomes every brand × every country. The chart still looks right, because the empty combinations carry no value, but the legend repeats each label once per combination. Which one do I need? Ask what the image or the color describes. "This is the Aurévia logo" — an attribute of the category, a column will do. "This is the flag of the market this chart is about" — an attribute of the legend, it has to be a measure. A measure is the safe answer in every case, and it is the only one that works on the Column Chart, Line Chart, Scatter Plot, Gradient Heatmap and Radar: only the Pie Chart declares the Series Color and Logo roles on its category axis, so only it accepts a column there. -- Attaches the value to the legend group, whatever the field wells contain Flag = CALCULATE ( MAX ( Markets[country_flag_base64] ), ALLEXCEPT ( Markets, Markets[market_name] ) )

Colors are resolved in this order (highest priority first): Per-series conditional formatting (fx) — Rules set in the Data Colors card Series Color data role — Hex codes from your data model Power BI theme palette — The theme's automatic color assignment Default fallback — Built-in 10-color array On the Radar and the Pie Chart the same field feeds only one dimension at a time: the threads or the axes on the radar, the slices or the series on the pie. The Apply colors to dropdown decides which, and the Data Colors card lists that same dimension.

Once logos are loaded via the Logo data role, they can appear in multiple places depending on the visual type: Legend — Every visual that has a Logo role supports logos in the legend. Set Legend Display to "Logo and Text" or "Logo" in the Legend formatting card. Inside bars — The Column Chart can display logos inside bars. Set Bar Logo Placement to Center, Top, or Bottom in the Bar Settings card. End-of-line labels — The Line Chart shows logos alongside end-of-line labels when the legend position is set to "End of Line". At the end of each axis — The Radar reads the same field per axis as well as per series. Set Axis Logo in the Axes card to Replace, Above, or Beside the label. In the small-multiple title — The Pie Chart reads the field per category for the legend and per legend value for the chart titles. Set Title Display in the Series Title card.

The following Python script scans a folder of image files and generates an Excel file with two columns: label (filename without extension) and logo (base64-encoded image). """ Convert a folder of logo images to an Excel lookup table. Usage: python logos_to_excel.py <logo_folder> [output.xlsx] Example: python logos_to_excel.py ./logos logos_table.xlsx """ import sys import os import base64 from pathlib import Path try: import openpyxl except ImportError: print("Install openpyxl first: pip install openpyxl") sys.exit(1) SUPPORTED_EXTENSIONS = {".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".gif", ".svg", ".webp"} MIME_TYPES = { ".png": "image/png", ".jpg": "image/jpeg", ".jpeg": "image/jpeg", ".gif": "image/gif", ".svg": "image/svg+xml", ".webp": "image/webp", } def image_to_base64(file_path: Path) -> str: """Read an image file and return a data URI base64 string.""" ext = file_path.suffix.lower() mime = MIME_TYPES.get(ext, "image/png") with open(file_path, "rb") as f: encoded = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8") return f"data:{mime};base64,{encoded}" def main(): if len(sys.argv) < 2: print(__doc__) sys.exit(1) logo_folder = Path(sys.argv[1]) output_file = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else "logos_table.xlsx" if not logo_folder.is_dir(): print(f"Error: '{logo_folder}' is not a valid directory.") sys.exit(1) # Collect image files images = sorted( f for f in logo_folder.iterdir() if f.is_file() and f.suffix.lower() in SUPPORTED_EXTENSIONS ) if not images: print(f"No image files found in '{logo_folder}'.") sys.exit(1) # Create Excel workbook wb = openpyxl.Workbook() ws = wb.active ws.title = "LogosColors" ws.append(["label", "logo"]) for img_path in images: label = img_path.stem # filename without extension logo_b64 = image_to_base64(img_path) ws.append([label, logo_b64]) print(f" Processed: {img_path.name} → {label}") wb.save(output_file) print(f"\nDone! {len(images)} logos exported to '{output_file}'.") if __name__ == "__main__": main() Performance Warning — Image Size Matters! Strongly recommended: resize your logo images before encoding them in base64. Power BI loads the base64 string for every single data point in the visual. If your logos are high-resolution photographs (e.g. 1024×1024 at 300 DPI), the data model will become extremely large and Power BI will slow down dramatically. Recommended settings for logos: Size: 32×32 to 64×64 pixels maximum Resolution: 72 DPI (screen resolution) Format: PNG with transparency, or SVG for vector logos File size: aim for under 5 KB per image after encoding A 64×64 PNG icon is typically 2–4 KB in base64, while a 512×512 photo can exceed 200 KB. With 10 series and 50 data points, that's the difference between 1 MB and 100 MB of data loaded into memory.

documents.t: The X Axis and Y Axis cards control the scale and labeling of the coordinate system on which the heatmap is plotted. Both axes are always numeric (continuous).

Both axes share the same set of options: Property Description Default Show Axis Show or hide the axis line, tick marks, and tick labels On Show Title Display an axis title On Title Custom title text (leave empty to use the field name from the data role) "" Range Min Manual lower bound for the axis scale (leave empty for auto) Auto Range Max Manual upper bound for the axis scale (leave empty for auto) Auto

When Range Min and Range Max are left empty, each axis is scaled to the extent of the X Axis or Y Axis data role values respectively, with a small padding added so the outermost sample points are not clipped against the plot border. Fixing the scale across pages If you use the heatmap across multiple report pages and want a consistent coordinate space, set explicit Range Min / Range Max values. This prevents the scale from jumping when the data changes between pages. Range and isolines The axis range also affects where isolines appear: the interpolation surface is only computed within the plotted area. Sample points outside the manual range are still used to compute the interpolation but their markers and labels will be clipped.
The Category Labels card controls text labels rendered near each sample point when a Categories data role is populated.
Property Description Default Show Show or hide all category labels Off

Property Description Default Font Family Label typeface Segoe UI Font Size Label size in pixels 11 px Bold Bold weight Off Italic Italic style Off Underline Underline decoration Off Color Label text color #222222
Property Description Default Word Wrap Automatically split long labels across multiple lines Off Max Width Maximum label width in pixels before wrapping 80 px

Property Description Default Background Show a filled rectangle behind each label On Background Color Fill color of the label background #FFFFFF Background Transparency Opacity of the background (0 % = fully opaque) 30%

Labels are positioned using a multi-pass algorithm designed to avoid overlaps even on dense point clouds: Occupation grid — a 4 px cell grid tracks occupied areas (other labels, sample markers, plot borders) Clustering — nearby points are grouped so cluster labels do not stack on top of each other Candidate generation — 32 candidate positions are tested along a spiral around each point Leader line detection — candidates that would require the leader line to cross another point or label are penalized Refinement pass — remaining leader-line/label collisions are resolved Swap pass — pairs of intersecting leader lines are uncrossed by swapping their label positions Pull-back pass — labels that overflow the plot boundary are pulled back inside Large datasets The placement algorithm runs entirely client-side at render time. For very large category counts (hundreds of distinct labels), consider increasing Font Size slightly and enabling Word Wrap with a short Max Width to reduce individual label footprints and give the algorithm more room to work. Leader lines Leader lines connect each label to its sample point marker. Their length and angle are determined by the placement algorithm; they are not configurable independently. Leader lines are automatically hidden when a label is placed close enough to its point that no connector is needed.
The Color Scale card controls the mapping from interpolated values to colors, including the color palette and the value range.

Five presets are available: Preset Description Viridis Perceptually uniform blue-green-yellow ramp; good for print and colorblind-safe use Turbo High-contrast rainbow ramp; emphasizes differences in the mid-range Red-Yellow-Blue Diverging palette; suited for data with a meaningful center point (e.g., deviation from a target) Spectral Similar diverging palette with a wider hue range Custom Define your own three-stop gradient using the Min, Mid, and Max color pickers Turbo Viridis Red-Yellow-Blue Spectral Custom

When Custom is selected, three color pickers become available (only visible when Custom is chosen in the Preset dropdown): Property Stop Description Min Color 0 (lowest value) Color at the bottom of the value range Mid Color 0.5 (midpoint) Color at the center of the range Max Color 1 (highest value) Color at the top of the value range Diverging custom scale For a diverging custom scale, set Mid Color to a neutral tone (e.g., white or light grey) and contrast Min and Max with two saturated hues such as blue and orange.

By default the range is derived automatically from the minimum and maximum values in the dataset. You can override it manually: Property Description Default Range Min Value mapped to the first color stop Auto (dataset minimum) Range Max Value mapped to the last color stop Auto (dataset maximum) Clamping Values outside the manual range are clamped to the nearest stop color — they are not hidden or excluded from the heatmap surface.

Property Description Default Transparency Global alpha of the heatmap canvas layer (0 % = fully opaque, 100 % = fully transparent) 0% Reducing transparency lets you layer the heatmap over a background image or other Power BI visuals while preserving spatial reference.
The Heatmap card controls how the interpolated surface is computed and rendered.

The visual estimates the value at every pixel by interpolating from the sample points. Three algorithms are available: Method Description Best For IDW (Inverse Distance Weighting) Each pixel is a weighted average of all samples; weight decreases with distance raised to a configurable power Sparse or irregular point clouds (tens to a few hundred points) Bilinear Builds a coarse IDW grid then interpolates each pixel from its 4 surrounding grid corners: v = v₀₀·(1−fx)·(1−fy) + v₁₀·fx·(1−fy) + v₀₁·(1−fx)·fy + v₁₁·fx·fy Any point density; produces a perfectly smooth surface with no blocky or faceted artifacts Triangulated Piecewise-linear interpolation over a Delaunay triangulation of the sample points Dense, regular grids (e.g. 50×50 or larger) where each triangle is only a few pixels wide RBF (Radial Basis Function) Gaussian-weighted Shepard interpolation with a bandwidth parameter that controls how far each sample's influence spreads Sparse data where each sample's influence should drop off sharply beyond a certain radius Choosing a method IDW is the safe default for any point cloud. Bilinear gives the same smoothness as IDW but with perfectly continuous color gradients across cell boundaries — often visually cleaner on dense data. Triangulated produces visible angular facets at low point counts (each Delaunay triangle boundary shows as a colour crease). It is best reserved for dense regular grids (100×100+) where the triangles are sub-pixel and the facets disappear. RBF is useful when you want each sample's influence to drop off quickly — tune RBF Bandwidth to control the radius.

Property Description Default Interpolation Method IDW, RBF, or Bilinear IDW IDW Power Exponent applied to distance in the IDW formula. Higher values make the influence of each point fall off faster, sharpening local peaks. 2 RBF Bandwidth Gaussian sigma expressed as a percentage of the shorter plot dimension. Smaller values create narrower influence zones; larger values smooth more aggressively. (Only visible when RBF is selected.) 15% Grid Resolution Side length (in pixels) of each interpolation cell. Smaller values produce a finer surface but increase render time. 4 px Minimum sample count At least 3 sample points are required to render the heatmap. With fewer points the visual displays an empty state message.
The Isolines card adds contour lines to the heatmap surface — curves that connect all points of equal interpolated value, similar to elevation contours on a topographic map.
Property Description Default Show Show or hide all contour lines Off

Property Description Default Count Number of isolines, distributed evenly across the value range 8 Color Stroke color of the contour lines #222222 Width Stroke width in pixels 0.8 px Transparency Opacity of the isoline strokes (0 % = fully opaque) 30%

Property Description Default Show Labels Display the interpolated value next to each contour line Off When enabled, labels float above the isoline with a lightly translucent background. The label placement engine: Avoids overlapping with category label rectangles already on the SVG Avoids overlapping with the plot borders Spaces labels along each contour at regular intervals Readable contours For a clean map-like appearance, set Count to 5–10, Transparency to around 30–40 %, and Width to 0.5–1 px. Enable Show Labels only when exact threshold values matter to the reader — they add noise at high counts. Isoline positions Isoline thresholds are evenly spaced between the effective Range Min and Range Max of the Color Scale. Changing the manual range will shift the isoline positions accordingly.
The Legend card controls the color bar that maps heatmap colors back to data values.
Property Description Default Show Show or hide the legend On
Property Description Default Position Where the legend is placed relative to the plot area: Right, Left, or Bottom Right

The legend displays an 18 px-wide gradient bar that reproduces the active color scale from the minimum to the maximum value. Five tick labels are drawn alongside the bar, evenly distributed across the range. Large values are automatically abbreviated: Range Displayed as ≥ 1 000 000 000 e.g. 1.2B ≥ 1 000 000 e.g. 3.5M ≥ 1 000 e.g. 42K < 1 000 Full number Position choice Right (default) — works well for wide visuals where vertical space is at a premium Left — mirrors the default, useful when the right side of the visual is crowded Bottom — best for tall or square visuals; the bar runs horizontally beneath the plot area
The Sample Points card controls the markers drawn at each original data point — the actual measurements from which the heatmap surface is interpolated.
Property Description Default Show Show or hide all sample point markers On
Property Description Default Shape Marker geometry: Circle, Square, Triangle, Diamond, Cross, Plus Circle Radius Marker radius in pixels 3 px

Property Description Default Use Heatmap Color Fill each marker with the interpolated heatmap color at its position, so it blends seamlessly with the surface On Color Fixed fill color used when Use Heatmap Color is off (hidden when Use Heatmap Color is on) #222222 Stroke Color Outline color drawn around each marker #333333 Visibility on dense surfaces When the heatmap surface is dense and saturated, markers with Use Heatmap Color on can be hard to spot. Disable it and choose a contrasting Color (e.g., white or black) to make sample locations clearly visible.

Sample points support full Power BI cross-filtering: Click a marker to select it and filter other visuals in the report Ctrl + Click (or Cmd + Click on macOS) to add to an existing selection Right-click to open the Power BI context menu Selected points stay at full opacity; unselected points are dimmed when a filter is active Hover to display a tooltip with X, Y, Value, Category, and any custom Tooltips measures

The SDM Gradient Heatmap renders a smooth, continuous color surface from a sparse set of XY sample points. Unlike tile-based heatmaps, values between samples are interpolated — the visual fills the entire plot area with a gradient rather than discrete colored cells.

Smooth interpolation — Three algorithms (IDW, RBF, Bilinear) to control how the surface is estimated between samples Color presets — Viridis, Turbo, Red-Yellow-Blue, Spectral, or fully custom min/mid/max colors Isolines — Contour lines at evenly-spaced value thresholds, with optional floating labels Sample point markers — Six shapes, configurable size, heatmap-derived or fixed colors Category labels — Smart multi-pass placement with leader lines, clustering, and word wrap Axes — X and Y axes with optional titles and manual range control Legend — Gradient color bar with auto-formatted tick labels (Right, Left, or Bottom) Cross-filtering — Click or Ctrl+click sample points to filter other visuals Tooltips — X, Y, Value, Category, and custom tooltip measures on hover

Data Role Description X Axis Numeric horizontal coordinate of each sample Y Axis Numeric vertical coordinate of each sample Value Numeric measure to interpolate across the surface (minimum 3 samples required) Categories Optional label/grouping field shown on sample point markers Tooltips Additional measures displayed in the hover tooltip

SDM visuals also support licensing through Microsoft Fabric subscriptions. When deployed in a Fabric workspace with an active subscription, the visual automatically detects the license level without requiring a manual key.
The line chart supports the same analytics features as the column chart, plus additional line-specific features.

Available in the Analytics pane: Y Constant Line — with configurable value (supports fx) Min Line, Max Line, Median Line, Average Line Each line supports styling (color, style, width, position) and optional shade areas.

A practical use of shade areas: enable both the Min Line and Max Line with their respective shade areas (shade below for Min, shade above for Max) to create a visual corridor that frames the data range. This clearly highlights the boundaries within which all data points fall.
Same four computation modes as the column chart: By Percentage, By Field, By Percentile, By Standard Deviation With bar (whisker), marker, band, and label display options.
The line chart additionally supports an Average Curve that plots the average across all series for each category point.

The line chart supports two data label placement modes: Force Vertical — Labels stacked vertically above each data point Smart Placement — Automatic positioning to minimize overlaps with horizontal displacement All data label settings (font, color, background, leader lines) support per-series customization through the "Apply settings to" dropdown. See the Data Labels formatting page for full details.

The Add. Table adds rows of values to the chart — one cell per category, centred on its point: a base, a mean coming from another measure, a score, a logo. It is the same feature as in the Column Chart, laid out as rows.

Drop one or more measures in the Add. Table data role. Each measure becomes one row. The measures are not drawn as lines; with a Legend, each measure is read once per category (the legend values are merged).

In Edit mode, hover over the visual and click the ⚙ icon (top right, next to the ⓘ icon). The editor opens with one entry per measure of the well: format (font, size, colour, style, header, row height), row box (border, background, shadow), logo, separator, warning thresholds (low / high, marker, value colour, pill) and critical threshold. It is the column chart's editor — see The column editor for every setting. The result is stored as JSON in the Add. Table card of the Format pane.

The Position of each row decides where it goes: Position Where the row is drawn After the chart (default) Under the X axis labels, and under the Base Row when it is shown Before the chart Above the plot area The row names are written in the left margin, left-aligned like the base row label, and truncated so they never cross the Y axis. The margin widens to hold them, up to a third of the visual.

Alert and critical thresholds work as in the Column Chart. On a line chart, a category blanked by a critical threshold: is left as a gap in every line — the missing values mode decides whether the line breaks or bridges it; shows no value in the Add. Table rows nor in the base row; shows the replacement message, if any, over the plot area at its place; keeps its label on the X axis. A blanked category still serves as a reference for the significance tests: vs. Preceding category compares with it even though it is hidden.
The Data Labels card controls value labels displayed near each data point. All data label settings support per-series customization through the "Apply settings to" dropdown.

At the top of the Data Labels card, a dropdown lets you choose which series to configure: All Series — Sets the default values for all series <Series Name> — Overrides settings for a specific series only Series without explicit overrides inherit the "All Series" defaults. This allows you, for example, to show labels only for a specific series, or use a different font size to highlight key data.

Property Description Default Data Labels Master toggle — enables or disables data labels globally Off Show (per series) Show labels for this series Follows global The master toggle at the top of the card turns data labels on or off entirely. Within each series, the Show toggle controls whether that specific series displays labels.
Property Description Default Placement Force Vertical, Smart Placement Force Vertical

Force Vertical — Labels are stacked vertically above each data point. When labels overlap, they are pushed downward. Best combined with opaque backgrounds for readability. Smart Placement — Labels are positioned intelligently to minimize overlaps. Labels may be placed above or below data points, and displaced horizontally when curves cross through the label area.

Property Description Default Font Font family Segoe UI Text Size Font size in pixels 10 Bold / Italic / Underline Text style toggles Off Color Label text color #333333 Use Series Color Color labels to match their series Off Transparency Text opacity (0–100%) 0% Display Units Auto, None, k (thousands), M (millions), Mds (billions) Auto The visual also respects the format string defined on each measure in your data model (number of decimal places, currency symbols, etc.). Use Series Color — a must-have for readability The Use Series Color option (available for both text color and background color) is one of the most impactful settings for chart readability. When enabled, each data label is colored to match its series, making it instantly clear which value belongs to which line — even on dense charts with many overlapping series. This feature is not available in the standard Power BI Line Chart and can dramatically improve the user experience. Combine it with a series-colored background (see below) for maximum clarity: each label gets a colored badge that stands out against any background.

Property Description Default Background Show a background rectangle behind labels Off Background Color Background fill color #FFFFFF Background Use Series Color Match background to series color Off Background Transparency Background opacity (0–100%) 20%

Leader lines connect displaced labels back to their data points, making it clear which value belongs to which point. Property Description Default Leader Lines Show leader lines for displaced labels On Leader Line Color Line color #999999 Leader Line Transparency Line opacity (0–100%) 0% Leader Line Style Solid, Dashed, Dotted Solid Leader Line Width Line width in pixels 1 Leader lines only appear for labels that have been displaced from their natural position (either by stacking or by smart placement).

The line chart supports all standard positions plus a unique option: Position Description Top Legend above the chart Bottom Legend below the chart Left Legend to the left Right Legend to the right End of Line Labels placed at the end of each line

When position is set to End of Line, series names are placed directly at the right end of each line: Automatic overlap prevention: When labels overlap vertically, they are spread apart evenly from the center of the cluster Lead lines: 3-segment connector lines link each label back to its data point, with configurable corner radius Staircase channels: When multiple lines converge, lead lines are routed through separate channels to prevent crossing

Property Description Default Lead Line Corner Radius Rounding of lead line corners (px) 0 Lead Line Thickness Line thickness (px) 1 Assign Series Color to Font Color — visual consistency matters Enable "Assign series color to font color" to color each end-of-line label with the same color as its series. This creates a strong visual link between the line and its label, making the chart much easier to read at a glance — especially when many series converge. Combined with the same option on data labels and the legend, this gives a fully color-consistent reading experience that is not available in standard Power BI charts.

When Logo data is provided, the legend supports three display modes: Text — Color indicator + series name (default) Logo and Text — Logo image + series name Logo — Logo image only In End of Line mode, logos appear next to the label text at the end of each line.

A legend box is bounded: 150 px wide when it sits on the left or the right, the width of the visual when it sits on top or below. Text Wrap decides what happens to a series name that does not fit. The Significance card runs up to three independent statistical tests over the chart and decorates the points whose difference from a reference is statistically significant. The maths is shared with the SDM Smart Table visual, so the two product lines always agree on the same data.

Significance testing needs a sample size, or a reference computed in the model. Bind a measure to the Base (sample size) data role or to the Significance reference role — with neither, the Significance card does not appear in the Format pane at all (the Base Row card needs the Base). Data Role Type Role in the test Base (sample size) Measure n for every test. Read per category, shared by all series at a given X. Required by every mode except an external reference that carries its own result. Standard Deviation Measure Per series and per point. When present, switches the test from proportions to means. Optional. Significance reference Measure One to three measures read by the External reference mode. Not drawn. Optional. Because the base is per category, all series compared at the same X use the same n.

The choice is automatic and made per comparison, not globally: Mean test — when both compared points carry a standard deviation. Proportion test — in every other case. The Match status line inside each test tells you which one applies, so you can confirm your setup at a glance. If your measure carries a percentage format string, its values are scaled from 0–100 back to 0–1 before the proportion test, so 45.3 % is tested as 0.453.

The card is organised into four groups: Group Contains Tests Significance Level, Variance Method, Value scale, the three mode dropdowns Test 1 / Test 2 / Test 3, and the debug toggle Test 1, Test 2, Test 3 Display options and the reference settings of each test The three tests are fully independent — different comparison modes, different display modes, different colors — and all of them can decorate the same point at the same time.

A difference is reported as significant when the absolute test statistic exceeds that value. The Variance Method only affects the proportion test — it chooses between a pooled standard error and a separate one. It is ignored when the mean test runs.

Each point is compared to the point immediately before it, inside its own series. The first category is never decorated — it has no predecessor.

The pattern designates a reference category. Inside each series independently, the reference is the first point whose category name matches; every point of that series is then compared to it. All series therefore use a reference at the same position on the X axis, but each with its own value. The reference point compares to itself, so it never carries a decoration. Typical use: a baseline wave, a control cell, a "Total" category.

The pattern designates a reference series. The reference is the first series whose name matches; at every X, all series are compared to that series at the same X. This mode needs a Legend field with at least two series. Both sides of the comparison use the base of the current category, since the base is shared per X. Pairing across series Series are paired by position in the category list, not by category name. This is the normal case in Power BI — all series share the same axis — but be aware of it if you build the visual from a source where series do not share the same categories.

The reference is not in the chart: it comes from a measure of the Significance reference role, evaluated by Power BI for each point — typically last year, a benchmark or another scope. The measure returns a small JSON ({"val", "n"}, {"val", "n", "stddev"}, {"ttest"} or {"signif"}) that tells the visual either what to test or the result to display. See External reference for the formats, the DAX examples and the status messages.

The field takes a JavaScript regular expression, evaluated case-insensitively and as a partial match — the pattern only has to appear somewhere in the name, it does not have to match the whole string. Pattern Matches 2009 2009, Q1 2009, 2009-T4 … ^2009$ exactly 2009 ^Total any name starting with Total Ref|Base any name containing Ref or Base Cat\. A Cat. A — the dot is escaped to mean a literal dot Remember that ., +, *, ?, (, ), [, ], {, }, ^, $, | and \ are regular expression operators and must be escaped with a backslash to be matched literally.

A test silently produces nothing — rather than an error — in all of these situations: the Base value is missing, zero or negative at one of the two points; either value is blank; the standard error works out to exactly zero; the regular expression matched nothing, or did not compile; in External reference mode, the reference measure is blank at that point, or its value is invalid — the status line counts them; in vs. Preceding category mode, on the first category of the axis; in Regular expression on X mode, on the reference point itself. Use the Match status line as your first diagnostic: it tells you whether the reference was resolved and which test is about to run.

For readers who need to reconcile the output with their own calculations. Proportion test — the statistic is z = (p₁ − p₂) / se, with Pooled Proportion: p = (n₁p₁ + n₂p₂) / (n₁ + n₂) and se = √( p(1−p) · (1/n₁ + 1/n₂) ) Separate: se = √( p₁(1−p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1−p₂)/n₂ ) Mean test — the statistic is t = (m₁ − m₂) / se, with se = √( s₁/n₁ + s₂/n₂ ) where s is the value supplied in the Standard Deviation role. Shared with the SDM Smart Table The mean test feeds the standard deviation directly into the variance slots of the standard error. This convention is inherited verbatim from the SDM Smart Table visual so that a line chart and a table built on the same measures always flag the same cells. If your reference implementation squares the standard deviation first, expect a difference on the mean test. In both cases the difference is reported as significant when |statistic| is strictly greater than the critical value of the chosen confidence level, and the sign of the difference selects the positive or negative decoration.

The Series Threshold card publishes, or withholds, one chart at a time. It asks of every series the question the Global Threshold asks of the whole visual — "is this base big enough to be shown?" — and answers it per small multiple, so a market with 40 respondents can be withdrawn while its neighbours keep being drawn. The left operand is never typed: it is the smallest base of the series, taken from the Base field well over the categories actually plotted. The card is therefore inert in a visual with no Base field — nothing is drawn, nothing is hidden. A threshold left at 0 switches its level off — the same convention as the Global Threshold, where both operands at 0 leave the conditional message disabled. That is what lets you use the warning alone, the hiding alone, or the two together as a graded rule: Warn below 80 ⚠ Low base (62) Hide below 50 Not shown — smallest base is under (50)

Property Description Default Warn below The series is flagged under this base 0 (off) Warning message Text shown under the chart while the warning holds ⚠ Low base (%BASE) Font / Text Color Appearance of the message Segoe UI 9 italic, #B06000 Background / Border Whether the message draws a filled and outlined box Off, off %BASE is replaced by the smallest base of that series. It is what makes the warning say which base is low rather than merely that one is — the number cannot come from a setting, since it differs from one small multiple to the next. The warning sits in a band reserved at the foot of every cell, never over the chart. The band is taken off every cell, including the ones carrying no warning: charts of different radii on the same grid would read as charts of different magnitudes.

The message that replaces a withdrawn chart is built from three fields, for the same reason the Note splits its caption in three — only the number has to come from the model: Property Description Default Hide below The series is withdrawn under this base 0 (off) Prefix Wording in front of the value Not shown — smallest base is under ( Value The number between the wordings (empty) Suffix Wording after the value ) Font / Text Color Appearance of the message Segoe UI 10, #C00000 Background / Border Whether the message draws a filled and outlined box On, on Prefix Not shown — smallest base is under ( Value (empty, or bound to a measure through fx) Suffix ) Not shown — smallest base is under (50) Value left empty writes the Hide below threshold — the number the sentence is about, and the one nobody should have to retype next to the setting that already carries it. Bind it through fx when the threshold lives in the model, or write %BASE in it to publish the base that was actually found instead of the rule that rejected it. The wording being an ordinary visual setting rather than a DAX measure leaves one place to translate per visual, which is the whole point of splitting the sentence up. Hiding without a message Clear Prefix, Value and Suffix and the chart is simply absent — the cell stays empty, the series title still names it. That is the discreet form of the same rule.

A withdrawn series keeps its series title: without it, an empty cell in the grid names nothing, and a reader cannot tell which market was withheld from one that was never in the report. Everything else goes — slices, data labels, target line, significance icons — and the cell stops responding to hover and to click, so a withdrawn series cannot be cross-filtered into another visual either.

Warn below and Hide below are both conditional-formatting fields. Bound to a measure through fx, they are evaluated inside each legend group, which gives one threshold per series — the publication rule of a country, read from the model rather than retyped in the visual. The value typed on the card stays the fallback for the series the measure says nothing about. The wordings work the same way, so a message can name the market it is about.

Global Threshold Series Threshold Note Scope the whole visual one series the whole visual What it does erases everything withdraws one chart, or flags it decorates, never removes Typical use nothing here may be published this market may not, the others may the base deserves a caveat The three stack cleanly: a Note carrying the overall base, a Series Threshold withdrawing the markets that fall short, and a Global Threshold for the case where the page filters leave nothing worth showing at all. Only on the Pie Chart The card is new and, for now, exposed by the Pie Chart alone. It needs a chart that is already split into one drawing per series, which is what the small multiples give it — that is also why the Column Chart solves the same problem differently, by hiding individual columns.
